t5sd-gto-short: Short-deck poker (ignoring rake) approximates a multiway non-zero-sum game, but heads-up short deck is still a two-player zero-sum game where the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee applies. The core difference from standard hold'em GTO is range and made-hand structure: higher pair density, bigger flush value, and common draws lead to higher equilibrium betting frequencies, higher bluff density, and clearer polarization.

Short-deck GTO is a "bulletproof vest": it guarantees you're not exploited but doesn't promise maximum profit. Against a leaky opponent, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. Short-deck pros switch between "wearing the vest" and "switching to the knife".

Short-deck value:bluff ratio and MDF (formulas unchanged, inputs adjusted):

Value:bluff ratio = b/(1+2b) (b = bet/pot ratio)
Full pot: 1/3 bluffs (2:1 value)
Half pot: 1/4 bluffs (3:1)

MDF = 1/(1+b): half pot defend 67%, full pot 50%

Short-deck adjustment points:
1. Higher made-hand value (flushes/straights) → value bets can use bigger sizes
2. Draws more common → bluff density can be a bit higher (semi-bluff with strong draws)
3. High pair density → defense ranges contain more pairs, supporting higher MDF

Concept from: Short Deck Poker GTO frequencies and 6+ structure

Short-deck GTO practice: because flushes/straights are highly valuable and draws common, short-deck betting ranges are more polarized (strong made hands + semi-bluff draws) and bet sizes can be larger (big bets extract made-hand value). But frequency balance remains core — value:bluff ratios and defensive MDF must be sound, or the opponent counters you.

Example: Short-deck river full-pot bet, equilibrium value:bluff ratio 2:1. You mix a flush (value) with a missed straight draw (bluff). If you only bet flushes (0% bluffs), the opponent folds everything to your full-pot bets and exploits you; if you bluff more than half, he calls everything and exploits you. The equilibrium ratio leaves the opponent torn.

Example 2 (minimum necessary deviation): You observe a short-deck opponent calls big river bets only 25% (equilibrium ~50%). Based on this you can raise your river overbet bluff frequency overall — but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%". That's "using GTO as the baseline and making disciplined deviations from observable biases".

Counterintuitive point: short-deck GTO isn't "playing tight" but "keeping everything at ratios the opponent can't counter". Short-deck GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves, and semi-bluffs — equilibrium frequencies just look more "aggressive" because made-hand value is high and draws are common.

Short-deck GTO learning path: first use a solver to understand the equilibrium "shape" (why play this way), then use node locking to study "harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate live. The baseline gives you invincibility; deviations give you profit.
t5sd-bluff: Short-Deck Bluffing: Higher Reward, Higher Risk

Short-deck bluffing has higher profit potential: because made hands (flushes/straights) are valuable and pots are usually big, a successful pot steal pays well; and opponents may fold more often given high draw density. But risk is higher too — calling ranges are wide and draws get there often, so your bluff is more likely to be "accidentally called into". The key to short-deck bluffing is semi-bluffing with strong draws to reduce risk.
Short-deck bluffing rule: prefer semi-bluffs with strong draws (flush/straight draws) over pure air. A semi-bluff has improvement room even when called, converting bluff risk into an investment.
The Math of Semi-Bluffs and Bluff Frequency

Short-deck semi-bluff EV (flop, strong draw):

EV(bluff) = f×P − (1−f)×(1−E_win)×Bet + (1−f)×E_win×(P+Bet)
(f = opponent fold rate, E_win = equity when called)

Versus pure-air bluff (E_win ≈ 0):
Pure air: EV = f×P − (1−f)×Bet
Semi-bluff: higher EV because of the E_win improvement room

Example: pot 8, bet 4, opponent folds 50%, your straight-draw equity when called is 35%:
EV(bluff) = 0.5×8 − 0.5×(0.65)×4 + 0.5×0.35×12 = 4 − 1.3 + 2.1 = 4.8

Semi-bluff EV 4.8 is clearly above pure air's EV = 0.5×8 − 0.5×4 = 2. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker semi-bluffs and the 6+ game)

Short-deck bluff-frequency practice: because flush/straight draws are common and made-hand value is high, short-deck bluffing ranges should be semi-bluff-heavy. Pure-air bluffs are risky in short deck (wide calling ranges, easily accidentally called into). Also optimize with blockers — holding A♠ blocking the opponent's nut flush raises bluff success.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♥9♥ on a K♥8♦6♣ flop. You have a flush draw (6 outs) + A high. The opponent bets and you raise as a semi-bluff: if he folds you win the pot directly; if he calls you have flush/overcard improvement room. Short-deck flush value is enormous, so this semi-bluff's EV far exceeds pure air.

Example 2 (blocker bluff): Short-deck flop K♠9♠6♠ (three spades), you hold A♠8♦ (lone A♠, no flush). You block every A♠X♠ nut-flush combo — the opponent's "strongest hand" is falsified. Raising to represent a flush now has a significantly higher success rate. A blocker turns the same "air" into a differently-strength bluff.

Counterintuitive point: pure-air bluffing in short deck is high-risk behavior. Because opponent draw density is high and calling ranges wide, your air bluff easily gets "accidentally called" or even outdrawn by a draw. Short-deck bluffs should be semi-bluff-heavy — convert risk into investment with strong draws.

Short-deck bluffing quick memory: prefer semi-bluffs (flush/straight draws), EV 2-3× pure air; holding an A blocking the nuts adds to bluffs; raise bluff frequency against high fold rates. Avoid mindless pure-air bluffing in short deck.
t5sd-mixed-strategy: Short-Deck Mixed Strategies: Same Equations, Different Inputs

The standard-track chapter "Mixed Strategies, the Indifference Principle and Node Locking" already gives the proof from first principles: a hand is split across several actions if and only if every one of those actions has exactly the same expected value. This chapter does not repeat that proof. It solves a translation problem instead — move the same equations onto a 36-card deck and ask which quantities carry over and which must be recomputed. The answer is a clean split: bet size determines frequencies, the deck determines equity.

Four quantities that depend only on bet size and are identical in both games:

Defence obligation MDF = P / (P+b):
  half pot 66.7%, pot size 50.0%, double pot 33.3%

Alpha, the threshold where a bluff stops being exploitable = b / (P+b):
  half pot 33.3%, pot size 50.0%, double pot 66.7%

The break-even fold rate of a bluff is the same expression read the other way round

Equity needed to call = amount to call / pot after you call:
  pot 8 facing a bet of 4: 4 / 16 = 25.0%

If the size stays the same, not one of these numbers moves — short deck does not shift the half-pot defence obligation away from 66.7%.
(Concept from: Modern Poker Theory, Ch.3 mixed strategies and indifference)

This gives the single most transferable judgement of the chapter: short deck needs no second set of frequency formulas. Whenever you are told that "MDF works differently in short deck", something about the size or the equity input was changed — not the indifference equation itself. Conflating the two means filing an input difference under "a different theory".
What the deck changes is equity and combo counts

Unknown cards in short deck = 36 - 2 hole cards - 3 community cards = 31 (30 after the turn), versus 47 / 46 in holdem.
A flush draw in short deck is always 5 outs (only 9 cards per suit, four already visible), versus 9 outs in holdem.

Exact two-street equity (1 - probability both streets miss):
  short deck 5 outs: 30.1%   short deck 8 outs: 45.6%
  holdem 9 outs: 35.0%

Single street:
  short deck 5 outs: 16.1%   short deck 8 outs: 25.8%   holdem 9 outs: 19.1%

Note that the short-deck flush draw is weaker in raw equity (about four points lower); the compensation sits on the value side once it does arrive — a flush ranks above a full house.

Worked example (the same indifference equation, opposite answers on two streets): pot 8, opponent bets 4, you call 4 making 16, so the threshold is 25.0% equity. On the flop your flush draw has two streets left: 30.1% > 25.0%, the call holds. On the turn the same draw has one street left: 16.1% < 25.0%, and the identical hand at the identical price flips from call to fold. Holdem with 9 outs also falls short on a single street (19.1%), so the rule is not short-deck specific; what is specific is that the two-street side only reaches 30.1%, shrinking the safety margin from ten points to five.

Since frequencies come from the equations and equities from the deck, every mixed node in short deck needs its inputs recomputed. Combo counts collapse just as sharply: with three spades on the flop, the chance that one given opponent holds at least one spade (already a flush) = 1 - C(27,2) / C(33,2) = 33.5%, and holding exactly two spades is only C(6,2) = 15 combos out of 528 (2.8%); the same calculation in holdem gives 37.0% and C(10,2) = 45 combos. Rarer made hands and fewer combos per draw are the other face of the same coin that puts a flush above a full house.

Worked example (splitting a frequency across a readable feature): flop Ks9s6s in short deck, you hold As8d. The solver may mix 60% raise / 40% call here. Humans cannot generate true randomness, so split it by an explainable feature: the branch holding As — which blocks the nut flush, since five of those 15 combos contain As and all drop to zero, leaving C(5,2) = 10 — raises 100%; the branch without it calls 100%. The overall frequency is unchanged, but each branch carries a stated reason, and execution error is far smaller than rolling dice in your head.

Counter-intuitive point: short-deck solver output looks more extreme than holdem — bigger sizes, higher frequencies — yet the indifference points at a given size sit exactly where they sit in holdem. Every difference comes from the inputs (equity and combo counts), not from the strategic principle. Memorising "short deck means playing aggressive" as a principle leads you to run the same frequencies in holdem and discover you are donating.
Data discipline for node locking in short deck

Node locking — freeze the opponent's observed tendency at a node, then re-solve your maximally exploitative response — only works if the tendency you lock comes from enough hands. The discipline is stricter in short deck: with fewer cards the outcomes cluster more sharply, so at the same sample size the observed frequency is noisier, and confirming one fold-rate leak takes no fewer hands than in holdem. As a rule of scale, hands required grow with (variance / edge) squared — halving the effect you are chasing costs four times the sample. The short-deck HUD baseline and its sample sizes are in this level's chapter "Short-Deck HUD Metrics and Sample Size".

Worked example: you notice a short-deck opponent folding 60% to half-pot continuation bets on the flop, while the defence obligation at that size is 66.7% — a systematic under-defence of 6.7 points. Locking that node and re-solving pushes your bluff frequency up and adds weak draws that would otherwise purely check. Hold on to the ceiling as well: the harvest is bounded by exactly those 6.7 points. An opponent under-defending by one point is not worth abandoning your baseline for, because the hole you open is bigger than the one you collect.

The computable part of the review routine (pot 8, bet 4):

Defence obligation MDF = 8 / (8+4) = 66.7%  ->  opponent measured at 60%, under-defending by 6.7 points
Break-even fold rate of a bluff = 4 / (8+4) = 33.3%  ->  at 60% folds you sit far above the profit line
So whether to bluff at all is never the question here; which hands to bluff with, and how wide to lock the range, is.

Run these two before you lock anything and you avoid the classic mistake — spending an already-profitable action to "exploit" an opponent who barely deviates.

One line to keep: size gives the frequency (MDF, Alpha and the break-even fold rate are identical in both games), the deck gives the equity (31/30 unknown cards, flush draws always 5 outs, made-hand combos collapse), and sample size gives the discipline (confirm you have enough hands before locking a tendency). Blur the three and you will file an input difference under "short deck has its own theory".

How to spend practice time: on a mixed node a single wrong pick costs almost zero expected value, so do not agonise over it. What is genuinely expensive is a wrong input — treating 5 outs as 9, reading the turn as if it were the flop, estimating short-deck combo counts with a 52-card deck. After each session review only the inputs you miscounted, not the frequencies you never had to decide.

t5sd-bluff-q1.question: The main reason short-deck bluffing rewards rise is:
options: High made-hand value and usually big pots, so successful pot steals pay well
t5sd-bluff-q1.explanation: Short-deck made hands (flushes/straights) are valuable and pots are big, so successful pot steals pay well.

options: Semi-bluffs have improvement room when called (equity E_win > 0)
t5sd-bluff-q3.explanation: A semi-bluff retains equity (flush/straight improvement) when called, giving higher EV.

options: It blocks the nut flush, raising bluff success
The opponent definitely has a flush
t5sd-bluff-q4.explanation: Holding A♠ zeros out the opponent's A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest calling hands and raising bluff success.

options: Opponent draw density is high and calling ranges wide, so you're easily accidentally called into
t5sd-bluff-q5.explanation: Short-deck opponents have high draw density and wide calling ranges — pure-air bluffs easily get accidentally called or even outdrawn.

t5sd-mixed-strategy-q1.question: Compared with holdem, the defence obligation MDF facing a half-pot bet in short deck is:
options: Lower, because the deck has only 36 cards
Higher, because there are more draws
Not derivable from the bet size
t5sd-mixed-strategy-q1.explanation: MDF depends only on pot and bet size, not on the deck; short deck changes the equity inputs, not the frequency equation.

t5sd-mixed-strategy-q2.explanation: Amount to call divided by the pot after you call: 4 / 16 = 25.0%.

t5sd-mixed-strategy-q3.question: With three cards to a suit on a short-deck flop, your flush draw is normally:
t5sd-mixed-strategy-q3.explanation: Short deck has only 9 cards per suit (6 through ace) and four are already visible, so a flush draw is always 5 outs rather than the 9 of holdem.

t5sd-mixed-strategy-q4.question: With three spades on the flop, how does the chance that one opponent holds at least one spade compare between short deck and holdem?
options: About 33.5% in short deck, below about 37.0% in holdem
About 37.0% in short deck, above 33.5% in holdem
t5sd-mixed-strategy-q4.explanation: Short deck: 1 - C(27,2)/C(33,2) = 33.5%; holdem: 1 - C(39,2)/C(49,2) = 37.0%. The smaller deck makes made flushes rarer per combo.

t5sd-mixed-strategy-q5.question: Before exploiting an opponent through node locking, the most important discipline is:
options: Confirming the tendency comes from a large enough sample
Locking the same node in a holdem solver first
Splitting the mixed frequency across suit features
t5sd-mixed-strategy-q5.explanation: A locked tendency must come from enough hands; short deck is noisier at the same sample size, and locking an imagined leak swaps your bulletproof vest for paper.
